Medical Neuroanatomy · Chapter 4 · Case Study 4-2

Medial Medullary Syndrome

43-year-old man with crossed (alternating) hemiplegia
Working dx: Left medial medullary infarct Vascular / stroke Brainstem localization

Chief Complaint

This was a 43-year-old, right-handed man with a chief complaint of headaches, slurred speech, and weakness in his right arm and leg.

History of Chief Complaint

The headaches began 3 weeks ago, and 2 weeks ago he noticed the onset of limb weakness and slurred speech. These symptoms resolved in 12 hours and recurred several times in the next 48 hours1. Twelve days ago the neurologic symptoms reappeared rapidly2. Currently, the headaches have abated, but the weakness and dysarthria remain3.

Medical History

The patient was an accountant in a large business firm and regularly worked 60 to 70 hours per week. He was being treated for hypertension, but admitted to recently decreasing his medications without the consent of his physician4. He had a 30-pack-year history of smoking5 and consumed several ounces of alcohol daily6. He denied the use of alcohol during the past 24 hours.

General Physical Examination

This was a stable, well-nourished, alert, oriented man who appeared his stated age. He could comprehend spoken and written language, but had dysarthria7. His speech was thickened, as if his tongue was swollen8. Heart sounds were normal, blood pressure was high (150/99)9. Pulse rate and respirations were normal; chest was clear to auscultation and percussion. Abdomen was soft with no lumps, masses, or tenderness.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status

He was alert and oriented with respect to person, time, and place. His speech was dysarthric; however, word-finding ability, comprehension, and repetition were all normal10. His reading and writing were appropriate. His fund of knowledge was intact.11

Cranial Nerves

His tongue deviated to the left on attempted protrusion12. The surface of the tongue on the left side was wrinkled, and muscular fasciculations were present13. All other cranial nerves were intact14.

Motor Systems

His right upper and lower limbs were noticeably weaker than those on the left15. He had elevated deep tendon reflexes in the right limbs and increased muscle tone in both right limbs16. A Babinski reflex was present on the right17. All other regions were intact.

Sensory

All sensory systems were intact. There was no loss of pinprick or thermal sensation, no loss of vibratory, discriminative sensation, and no loss of proprioception throughout his body.18

Follow-up

Re-examination at 3 months following discharge finds that his speech has completely cleared and gross motor strength has returned to normal19. His deep tendon reflexes remain elevated on the right upper and lower extremities20.

Discussion Questions

As posed in the source case — the Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough below works through these directly.
  1. Has the patient experienced any changes in consciousness or cognition, language function or spatial recognition, personality or emotional behavior, or any loss in memory?
  2. Does the patient exhibit any loss of vision and if so, where in the visual field is the loss? Are there any visual hallucinations present in this patient?
  3. Are there any changes in cranial nerve function and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  4. Are there any changes in motor function such as reflexes, muscle tone, movement, or coordination and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  5. Are there any changes in sensory function and if so, what levels of the body have experienced this change?
  6. What is the clinical temporal profile of this patient's neurologic problem: is the onset of neurologic findings acute or insidious? Is the course of the neurologic disease chronically progressive, fluctuant, or stable?
  7. Based on the presenting signs and symptoms, do you think the distribution of the neurologic pathology is focal, multifocal, or diffuse?
  8. Based on the answers to these questions, develop a differential diagnosis of the patient's neurological problem.
  9. If the origin of the pathology is vascular, what arterial supply is most likely involved with the lesion in this patient?
Synthesis

Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough

1 · Localization

Left medulla, at the pyramidal decussation

The exam combines a left-sided lower motor neuron CN XII deficit (tongue deviates left, with atrophy and fasciculations) with a right-sided upper motor neuron limb deficit (spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, increased tone, Babinski sign). Because the corticospinal tract has already crossed by the time it reaches the caudal medulla, a single left-sided lesion at or just above the pyramidal decussation explains both findings at once — a pattern called inferior alternating hemiplegia. Fully preserved language, reading, writing, and fund of knowledge argue against any cortical contribution, so this is a segmental brainstem lesion, not a suprasegmental one.

2 · Distribution

Focal — anterior (medial) zone

Findings cluster tightly around one territory rather than appearing scattered. The complete absence of lateral-zone signs (no facial sensory loss, no dysphagia, no vertigo or ataxia) and posterior-zone signs (sensation is fully intact) argues for a focal process restricted mainly to the anterior zone — the pyramid and hypoglossal fascicle — while sparing the medial lemniscus.

3 · Time Course

Crescendo TIAs → completed infarct

Two phases: first, transient episodes that fully resolved within 12 hours and recurred repeatedly over 48 hours — the signature of intermittent ischemia in a penetrating-artery territory. Then, 12 days ago, the deficit reappeared and this time became fixed. This TIA-to-completed-infarct evolution over roughly two weeks is classic for small-vessel occlusive vascular disease, not a single abrupt catastrophe or a slowly progressive process. Once fixed, the course has been stable — no further fluctuation, no progression — which the small group shorthanded as simply "acute, then stable."

4 · Differential Diagnosis

Leading diagnosis: Medial Medullary Syndrome (left)

DiagnosisFitsArgues against
Medial Medullary SyndromeMost likely Crossed picture — ipsilateral CN XII LMN signs + contralateral limb UMN signs; heavy vascular risk-factor burden (undertreated HTN, 30-pack-yr smoking, daily heavy alcohol use); crescendo-TIA pattern typical of penetrating-artery ischemia. The full triad can also include contralateral loss of tactile/proprioceptive sense when the lesion extends far enough laterally to reach the medial lemniscus — absent here, consistent with a smaller lesion restricted to the pyramid and hypoglossal fascicle rather than arguing against the diagnosis itself.
Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Wallenberg) Also a vascular medullary syndrome with an acute-on-subacute vertebrobasilar presentation. No facial sensory loss, no Horner's syndrome, no dysphagia/hoarseness, no vertigo, diplopia, or limb ataxia — none of the lateral-zone features are present.
Unilateral (hemi-)medullary syndrome Complete vertebral artery occlusion can knock out all three medullary zones on one side at once. Exam shows no lateral- or posterior-zone findings at all, so a pure medial (anterior-zone) pattern fits far better than a combined one.
Demyelinating event (e.g., MS plaque) Can produce a relapsing-remitting focal brainstem deficit. Vascular risk-factor burden, single well-localized event with no other CNS episodes, and a TIA-then-stroke evolution are all far more typical of ischemia than demyelination.
5 · Diagnostic Workup

From emergent imaging to secondary prevention

  1. Thrombolysis-window check (moot here, but the first question asked).Thrombolytic therapy requires a witnessed onset within roughly 4.5–6 hours. At 12 days out with a fluctuating history, he is nowhere near eligible — but this is the very first thing the small group said to check for a fresh presentation.
  2. Emergent noncontrast head CT.Rules out hemorrhage first — important given his uncontrolled BP (150/99) and recent antihypertensive nonadherence, before anything else proceeds.
  3. MRI brain with DWI/ADC.Gold standard for an acute medullary infarct; expect restricted diffusion in the left anteromedial medulla. CT alone often misses posterior-fossa infarcts due to bone artifact.
  4. MRA/CTA of the head and neck.Vessel imaging of the vertebral and anterior spinal arteries — looking for stenosis, occlusion, or dissection at the level of the medulla.
  5. Cardiac workup (ECG ± echocardiogram).Still reasonable to screen for a cardioembolic source, though the crescendo-TIA pattern and perforating-vessel anatomy here point more toward small-vessel (lipohyalinotic) disease than embolism — see the mechanism card below.
  6. Vascular risk-factor labs.Fasting lipid panel, HbA1c/glucose, CBC — standard secondary-prevention stroke workup.
  7. Address modifiable risk factors immediately.Restart/optimize antihypertensive therapy, smoking-cessation counseling, and alcohol-use counseling.
6 · Prognosis

Generally favorable

Isolated medial medullary infarcts, especially small and unilateral ones that spare the sensory pathways, tend to have relatively good functional recovery — consistent with this patient's near-complete resolution of dysarthria and limb weakness by 3 months. The mechanistic reason (see the "Axons Die — Neurons Usually Don't" card below): in a small lacunar infarct, only the very center of the lesion is truly necrotic, while surrounding axons merely lose their myelin and can recover once remyelinated. Persistent hyperreflexia is a common residual finding and can outlast functional recovery. Bilateral medial medullary infarcts are rare but carry a worse prognosis, including risk of respiratory compromise from bilateral pyramidal involvement.

7 · Management

Supportive care → secondary prevention

  • Acute stroke protocol / thrombolysis-eligibility assessment at first fixed presentation
  • Speech-language pathology evaluation for dysarthria
  • Physical and occupational therapy for right-sided weakness and gait training
  • Fall precautions given limb weakness and increased tone
  • Optimize antihypertensive regimen and reinforce medication adherence
  • Smoking-cessation counseling and pharmacotherapy
  • Alcohol-use counseling and reduction
  • Antiplatelet therapy for secondary stroke prevention
  • Statin therapy per lipid workup
  • Longitudinal neurology follow-up to track recovery and residual reflex changes
Underlying Neuroanatomy

Concept Deep-Dive

Vascular anatomy

Medullary Vascular Zones

Anterior — ASA / VA medial branches Lateral — VA / PICA lateral branches Posterior — PSA / PICA posterior branches
This patient's deficits map almost entirely to the anterior zone: hypoglossal and corticospinal tract involvement, with sensation (medial lemniscus) spared and no lateral-zone signs at all — pointing to a small, discrete infarct centered on that single zone.
From the small group Mechanism

Small Vessel, Not Embolic — Why It Matters

Types of ischemic stroke — embolic, lacunar, atherothrombotic

This is textbook small-vessel (lacunar) disease, not an embolic stroke. The teaching point from the small group: penetrating branches like the medial medullary perforators come off their parent artery at right angles, while emboli tend to travel straight down the path of least resistance — so emboli largely bypass these tiny perforators. What actually narrows and eventually occludes them is chronic hypertension driving lipohyalinosis: lipid deposition and smooth-muscle thickening in the vessel wall. "Lacune" literally means little lake — the old descriptive term for the small fluid-filled cavity these infarcts leave behind once the tissue resorbs.

This reframes the workup: cardiac/embolic sources are still worth screening, but the primary driver here is his own vessel wall pathology from years of poorly controlled hypertension — which is exactly the risk factor he'd stopped treating.
From the small group CN XII

Nucleus, Radiations, or Nerve? — and Why the Tongue Deviates Left

Left: Netter illustration, sites of hypoglossal (CN XII) lesions · Right: clinical photo, tongue deviation with atrophy on protrusion

A flaccid (LMN) tongue palsy can come from three places: the nucleus, the radiations (axons crossing the brainstem to exit as the nerve), or the nerve itself. The small group worked through eliminating each one:

  • Not the nerve — an isolated peripheral CN XII lesion wouldn't touch the limbs. This patient also has right-sided upper- and lower-extremity findings, so something in the brainstem has to explain both.
  • Not the nucleus alone — the limb findings are spastic/UMN, not flaccid, so the corticospinal fibers are damaged in transit, not at their cell bodies.
  • Radiations, most likely — the hypoglossal radiations run medially, right alongside the corticospinal (pyramidal) fibers at this level, so a single small lesion there catches both systems at once. That anatomic proximity is the whole reason this syndrome exists as a recognizable pattern.
The unopposed, intact right genioglossus pushes the tongue tip toward the weak left side — in a lower motor neuron CN XII lesion, the tongue always deviates toward the side of the lesion. Left deviation, atrophy, and fasciculations together point to the left hypoglossal radiations, exactly where they run beside the pyramid.
Corticospinal tract

The Pyramidal Decussation

Because his weakness is right-sided and his tongue findings are left-sided, the lesion must sit on the left, above the pyramidal decussation — the only single location that produces this exact crossed pattern.
Sign pattern

UMN vs. LMN Signs — Where They Show Up Matters

Upper motor neuronLower motor neuron
StrengthWeak, spasticWeak, flaccid
ReflexesHyperreflexicHyporeflexic / absent
ToneIncreasedDecreased
BulkPreserved (early)Atrophy
Extra signsBabinski presentFasciculations
This patientRight limbsLeft tongue (CN XII)
This patient shows LMN signs in the tongue (ipsilateral to the lesion) and UMN signs in the limbs (contralateral to the lesion) at the same time — a reminder that where you find each sign type, not just their presence, is what does the localizing.
Differential anatomy

Medial vs. Lateral Medullary Syndrome

FeatureMedialLateral
Key structuresPyramid, medial lemniscus, MLF, CN XIINucleus ambiguus, spinal CN V, ALS, vestibular nuclei
MotorContralateral spastic hemiparesisUsually spared
TongueIpsilateral LMN CN XII palsySpared
SensoryContralateral proprioception/vibration lossIpsilateral face + contralateral body pain/temp loss

This patientMatches the medial column almost point-for-point; fails nearly every lateral feature
Lining his exam up against both columns is exactly why medial medullary syndrome, not Wallenberg syndrome, is the leading diagnosis here. From the small group
Medial medullary syndrome is a spectrum, not all-or-nothing — a bigger lesion can extend laterally enough to reach the medial lemniscus and add contralateral epicritic sensory loss. This patient's fully intact sensation says the lesion stayed small and restricted to the pyramid and hypoglossal fascicle.
Prognosis mechanism

Axons Die — Neurons Usually Don't

In a small lacunar infarct, only the very center of the lesion goes truly necrotic — those axons die outright (a form of Wallerian-type degeneration inside the CNS). Axons in the surrounding, less-severely-ischemic tissue lose their myelin and stop functioning, but the axon itself survives. Because the neuron cell bodies (cortex, hypoglossal nucleus) are untouched, oligodendrocytes can remyelinate those surviving axons and function can return.

This is the mechanistic reason a small lacunar infarct like this one has a good prognosis: most of the deficit is reversible demyelination, not permanent axon loss — consistent with this patient's near-complete recovery by 3 months, with only mild residual hyperreflexia marking where the true necrotic core was.
Time course

From Crescendo TIAs to a Fixed Deficit

The stepwise progression — fluctuating deficits that fully resolve, recur, then finally become fixed — is itself a diagnostic clue. It's the pattern expected when a penetrating artery is intermittently, then completely, compromised, rather than a single sudden large-vessel event or a slowly progressive tumor.
From the small group
Cross-Sectional Anatomy

Walking Down the Medulla, Plate by Plate

The small group worked through these exact labeled sections, level by level, to find where a single lesion could explain both the tongue and limb findings. The bottom two plates are the level of this patient's infarct — hypoglossal nucleus sitting right beside the pyramid.

Level 1 · Above the lesion

Cervical-Medullary Junction

  • LCST — lateral corticospinal tract, just settling into its final position
  • FC / FG — fasciculus cuneatus / gracilis (touch, vibration, proprioception on the way up)
  • STT / STN — spinal trigeminal tract / nucleus
  • ALS — anterolateral system (pain, temperature)
  • DSCT — dorsal spinocerebellar tract
  • Medial motor neurons here run neck/paraspinal and trapezius muscles — too high to be this patient's lesion.
Level 2 · The lesion level

Mid-Medulla (Plate 08)

  • XII — hypoglossal nucleus, sitting almost on the midline
  • MP — medial pyramid, corticospinal fibers, right beside XII
  • NA — nucleus ambiguus (laryngeal/pharyngeal muscles — CN IX/X)
  • DMN — dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
  • ML — medial lemniscus, formed here by internal arcuate fibers arcing across the midline
  • This is the level: XII and the pyramid are close enough that one small lesion catches both.
Level 3 · Same level, functional grouping

Mid-Medulla (Plate 09)

  • Somatic motor (medial): XII, DMN
  • Vestibular / somatic sensory: VN, LCN
  • Visceral sensory: SN (solitary nucleus)
  • Somatosensory: ML, STT/STN, ALS
  • Same structures as Plate 08, grouped by function instead of position — useful for predicting what a lesion here would and wouldn't touch.
From the small group
Why Sensation Was (And Wasn't) At Risk Here

Conscious vs. Unconscious Proprioception

This patient's sensory exam was completely normal — but the pathway that carries conscious proprioception (the medial lemniscus) runs immediately next to the structures that were damaged. The small group used this same session to build out the full proprioceptive circuit, which is exactly what a slightly bigger version of this lesion would have taken out.

DSCT origin

Clarke's Nucleus vs. the "Non-Clarke's" Route

Below C8, muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ afferents synapse in the dorsal nucleus of Clarke (C8–L3) before ascending to the cerebellum. Above C8 — for the upper extremity — there's no Clarke's nucleus to synapse in, so those fibers ride up the fasciculus cuneatus instead and synapse in the external (accessory) cuneate nucleus in the medulla, the "non-Clarke's" equivalent.

The professor's framing: this is unconscious proprioception — the cerebellum gets constant feedback on limb position but never passes it to the cortex.
Conscious vs. unconscious

Two Circuits, One Set of Receptors

The same muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ signal splits: one branch drives the stretch reflex locally, a collateral heads to the spinocerebellar tract (unconscious), and — via the external cuneate nucleus — a copy also crosses into the medial lemniscus (conscious). As the small group put it: the cerebellum is "secretive" — it keeps its own copy of the data and calculates movement without ever reporting back to the cortex.

You're consciously aware of limb position only because conscious proprioception "taps into the cable" carrying the cerebellum's unconscious feed, via those internal arcuate fibers joining the medial lemniscus.
Full circuit

From Joint Receptor to Cortex

Conscious proprioception ascends via the dorsal columns, decussates as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus at the caudal medulla, and continues uncrossed from there up to the thalamus and somatosensory cortex. Unconscious proprioception peels off to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle and never reaches the thalamus at all.

This is the exact pathway that runs beside — but was spared in — this patient's lesion. A slightly larger infarct extending just a bit more laterally would have caught the medial lemniscus and produced contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception on top of everything else.
By spinal level

Where Each Segment's Signal Enters

Lower-body (thoracic/lumbar) Golgi tendon organ, muscle spindle, and joint-receptor input travels up the dorsal spinocerebellar tract. Upper-body (cervical) input takes the cuneocerebellar tract through the accessory cuneate nucleus instead — the same "non-Clarke's" route, just for the arm rather than the leg.

Two parallel unconscious-proprioception tracts, split by body region, both converging on the ipsilateral cerebellum.
Putting it together

The Dorsal Spinocerebellar Tract, Start to Finish

Traced from a muscle spindle below L3, up through the dorsal nucleus of Clarke, into the dorsal spinocerebellar tract, through the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the ipsilateral cerebellum and lateral cuneate nucleus — and, via a parallel branch, across the internal arcuate fibers into the medial lemniscus and up to the thalamus and cortex. One diagram, both the conscious and unconscious routes.

Everything this patient's exam ruled out (sensory loss) and everything it confirmed (tongue + limb findings) can be located on this one map, one structure at a time.
Bonus · from the same session, one level rostral — not part of this patient's findings

The Pons & the MLF

Right after finishing this case, the small group moved one level up to the pontomedullary junction and traced the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) — the tract connecting CN III, IV, and VI to the vestibular nuclei and down into the cervical cord, running the length of the floor of the 4th ventricle. It coordinates the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), keeping the eyes fixed on a target while the head moves.

Because it sits right against the 4th ventricle, the MLF is a favorite target for MS plaques. Damage causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO): impaired adduction of the affected eye on lateral gaze, with nystagmus in the abducting eye.
